title: Jael (Judges 4:17–22, 5:24)
hook: the woman of the tent ends the war; her song calls her blessed above women in the tent

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barak, and Deborah's short answer: I will surely go with thee. Your line was I will go with you. Today, the woman Deborah spoke of.

The battle is lost, the army is broken, and the great captain is running on foot. Sisera, who had oppressed Israel with chariots of iron, has jumped down from his own and fled. He's heading for safety: the tent of Heber the Kenite, whose house is at peace with his king. A woman steps out of the tent to meet him. "Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; fear not." Her name is Jael. Deborah said the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. The story has been waiting to show whose.
screen: `THE CAPTAIN RUNS ON FOOT.` → `A TENT AT PEACE WITH HIS KING.` → `TURN IN, MY LORD; FEAR NOT.`

segments.voice: Jael is an outsider to the story: the wife of Heber the Kenite, from a household that had moved away from its kin and made peace with Israel's enemy. No army, no title, no prophecy. She has a tent. And the text tells what happens inside it slowly, almost gently. She covers Sisera with a blanket. He asks for a little water; she opens a skin of milk, gives him a drink, and covers him again. He tells her to stand at the door: if anyone asks, is there a man here, say no. He falls asleep, worn out. Then she takes a tent peg and a hammer, the tools of her own home, and the war ends in her tent. When Barak arrives in pursuit, she goes out to meet him: come, I'll show you the man you're looking for. Deborah's words come true, through a woman nobody in the story was watching. Readers have felt both sides of this story. Some are troubled: she welcomed him, said fear not, gave him milk, and then killed him. Others see a woman who ended a long oppression with the only tools in reach. The text gives the last word to a song, where Deborah and Barak sing: "Blessed above women shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be, blessed shall she be above women in the tent." Not above women in palaces. Above women in the tent. Her place, the one nobody counted, is where the song blesses her.
screen: `AN OUTSIDER WITH A TENT.` · `MILK, A BLANKET, A PEG, A HAMMER.` · `READERS FEEL BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `BLESSED ABOVE WOMEN IN THE TENT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose work happens out of sight: someone who cleans, cooks, fixes, cares, keeps the records, holds the family together. Picture them in their own place and think of one specific thing they did that mattered. The song blessed Jael in her own tent; let your thought honor them in theirs.
Jael. The wife of Heber the Kenite, who met Sisera at her tent door, fulfilled Deborah's word, and is blessed in the song above women in the tent. Today's word.
Your line: blessed in the tent. Ed, the choice at Shechem, the cycle, Ehud, shofet, Barak and Jael: that's the week. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read Jael's story in Judges 4 and her praise in the Song of Deborah in Judges 5, and commentators discuss how to understand her welcome of Sisera.

chat.says: Is Jael a hero or a villain? She killed a guest in her tent.
options: Readers feel both sides; the song itself blesses her above women in the tent.
A villain: the Bible condemns her for breaking the rules of hospitality.
A hero only because Deborah had ordered her to do it beforehand.

Jael.meaning: the wife of Heber the Kenite, at whose tent the war ended

Sisera.meaning: the Canaanite captain who fled on foot

Heber.meaning: Jael's husband, whose household was at peace with Sisera's king

Kenite.meaning: from the Kenites, a clan living among Israel

Barak.meaning: the soldier who led Israel's army with Deborah
